evaluations.label: A
errors: “Working design presentation not yet on the server” identifies the wrong missing presentation. The industrial designer confirmed uploading that presentation, and participants could see it. The project manager's presentation was the one others could not see.

“Save from email into shared folder” presents an unconfirmed remedy as an instruction. The marketing expert suggested saving the emailed presentation, then retracted that suggestion; the project manager agreed to figure out the issue.

The agreed locator feature is specified as a “button on TV to make remote beep.” That was an example proposed by the project manager, not an agreed implementation. The agreement was to provide a way to prevent or address losing the remote.
“Target group: broad appeal, roughly under 65” makes the age boundary sound more settled than it was. Under 65 was one proposal; the discussion ended without an agreed age range.

Listing a “rechargeable or long-life battery solution” among agreed functions blurs the distinction between the desired long-lasting power source and the rechargeable cradle, which remained an exploratory idea.
strengths: Captures the main research statistics, the €25 selling price, and the €12.50 production ceiling.
Clearly organizes the scope restrictions, branding requirements, essential controls, secondary controls, and simplicity/fashion priorities.
Includes the individual workstreams, questionnaire and summary, coach instructions, and conditional sharing of additional demographic data.
Generally distinguishes exploratory ideas such as the LCD screen and charging cradle from the main design direction.
weaknesses: The incorrect shared-folder action could send someone to fix the wrong presentation.
Several tentative proposals become more definite in the target-group and agreed-functions sections.
Does not clearly assign the project manager's responsibility for posting minutes and documentation, and some other tasks lack explicit role owners.
Omits useful interface-design discussion about prototype feedback and balancing familiar layouts with distinctive design.

evaluations.label: B
errors: “Management decided against including teletext support or voice recognition” wrongly attributes the voice-recognition decision to management. Management excluded teletext; meeting participants argued against voice recognition because of cost and limited need.
Attributes potential LCD screens to the technical-interface speaker. The marketing expert raised the LCD possibility, not the user interface designer's technical-functions presentation.
“Action Items: (none)” contradicts the assigned questionnaires and summaries, individual concept work, market-trend watching, and documentation uploads.

Introduces “Would adding a ‘find my remote’ beep function fit within budget?” as an unresolved meeting question. Locator-specific budget feasibility was not discussed, and the general lost-remote finding function was agreed.
Says the charging cradle could improve “location tracking.” The discussion proposed keeping the remote in a regular storage location, not a tracking capability.
strengths: Provides substantial coverage of all three presentations, including prototype feedback, conventional layouts, and the trade-off between basic and fully featured remotes.
Accurately includes the television-only scope, branding requirements, production ceiling, selling price, and main research percentages.
The outline correctly records large essential buttons, less-prominent secondary controls, and a lost-remote finding function.
Describes the target demographic as a discussion rather than declaring a final age range.
weaknesses: Omits practically all closing assignments and follow-up responsibilities, despite declaring that there were no action items.
Does not document the presentation-sharing problem or the project manager's commitment to resolve it.
The summary introduces uncertainty about the locator requirement that the later outline records as agreed.
Uses unexplained numbered speakers instead of the transcript's role labels.
Repeats much of the summary in the outline without providing the missing operational next steps.

evaluations.label: C
strengths: Most faithfully distinguishes agreed requirements from proposals: age targeting remains unsettled, the sliding panel is a possible implementation, and the charging cradle remains exploratory.
Accurately captures the research findings, both price figures, television-only scope, teletext exclusion, corporate colors, and slogan.
Records the agreed loss-finding requirement without inventing a final mechanism.
Correctly identifies the working-design presentation as uploaded and the project manager's presentation as the unresolved shared-folder issue.
Includes useful timestamps and covers the interface-prototyping and familiar-versus-distinctive design discussion.
weaknesses: The action-item list includes only the project manager's documentation tasks, although other work is mentioned in the body.
Does not explicitly map the industrial designer to the components concept, the user interface designer to the interface concept, and the marketing expert to market-trend watching.
Omits the marketing expert's conditional commitment to email additional age data before the next meeting.
Omits the request that everyone upload their slides, the 30-minute individual-work period, and the instruction to record frustrations or issues in the summary.
Uses “Speaker 1” for action ownership rather than the clearer “Project Manager.”

evaluations.label: D
errors: “Target group 15–35 years” incorrectly presents a proposed age range as the final target. Its basis was voice-recognition interest, and the group subsequently left age targeting unresolved.

“Provide updated market research data” is listed as an unassigned, unconditional action. The marketing expert specifically offered to email additional age figures before the next meeting only if more figures became available.
“Investigate technical feasibility for rechargeable battery” is presented as an action item, but nobody was assigned that investigation. A rechargeable cradle was an idea to retain for consideration.
strengths: Concise coverage of the main research findings, common controls, interface simplification, and working-design components.
Correctly records the television-only scope, teletext exclusion, corporate colors, and production-cost ceiling.
Captures the core priorities of simplicity and fashion, large essential buttons, less-visible advanced controls, and addressing remote loss.
Keeps the rechargeable cradle as a possibility in the main notes and mentions living-room space constraints.
weaknesses: The incorrect target-age statement could materially misdirect subsequent design and marketing work.
The action list omits actual assignments while promoting an exploratory battery idea into a task.
Does not record the questionnaire and summary, role-specific concept work, coach emails, documentation uploads, or the missing presentation issue.
Omits the €25 selling price, the 100-person research sample, RSI concerns, and the corporate slogan.
Does not preserve the discussion of needs or purchasing capacity as alternatives to age-based targeting.

rationale: Overall scores are the equally weighted averages of the four criterion scores. C ranks first for source fidelity and careful separation of decisions from exploratory ideas, although its action coverage is incomplete. A is comprehensive and practical but misidentifies the missing presentation and overstates several proposals. B covers the presentations well but falsely reports no actions and introduces attribution and decision-status errors. D is concise but incorrectly fixes the target age range and replaces actual follow-up assignments with incomplete or unsupported tasks. Infrared's stated lack of a line-of-sight requirement is not penalized because that claim appears in the authoritative transcript.
